title: 2027-05-11 Quantization Technical Review - Venturi AI
summary: Deep technical review of quantization options for Venturi's LLM serving: tradeoffs between INT8/FP8 and GPTQ/AWQ, observed accuracy regressions on safety prompts, runtime impacts on latency/throughput, KV-cache and batching interactions, and VPC/on-prem deployment requirements including KMS integration. Agreed next steps to run targeted benchmarks and share quantization profiles and security docs.
topics: KV cache behavior with quantized models
action_items: Liam Chen: provide AWQ vs GPTQ micro-benchmark results (due 2027-05-18)
Ethan Miles: share sample inference traffic profile and p95/p99 latency targets (due 2027-05-14)
Ava Martinez: send security + deployment checklist, SOC2 docs, and pricing sheet (due 2027-05-13)
Sofia Kim: provide example long-prefix conversation test cases (due 2027-05-16)
next_steps: Run 1-week POC with GPTQ-INT8 variant on dedicated pool for Venturi
Redwood to run KV-cache regression test with 1k prefix length and share results and traces
Schedule follow-up call with Venturi SREs to review perf numbers (week of 2027-05-24)
Share benchmark spreadsheet and quant profiles (link provided in chat)
transcript: [00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll kick off the quantization deep dive. Priya, Ethan, Sofia, can you confirm audio?
[00:06] Dr. Priya Rao: Yeah audible here, thanks. We want to focus on INT8 + FP8 tradeoffs and GPTQ versus AWQ path, especially where we saw subtle accuracy regressions on our safety prompts.
[00:18] Liam Chen: Great, quick agenda: cover model-level accuracy findings, runtime/latency impacts, KV cache interactions, batching, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Leave time for Q&A.
[00:30] Ethan Miles: Quick context: our traffic is bursty, p95 latency target is ~120ms for small chat completions, and we have strict data residency and KMS requirements for keys used in tokens.
[00:45] Ava Martinez: Noted. We'll show where quantization gives cost/throughput wins versus where it costs you quality.

[01:05] Liam Chen: Starting with INT8: it's mature on our runtime. In our internal runs we saw 2.5-3x throughput on A100-like hardware for many decoder-only models with short sequences. But INT8 tends to hit issues on out-of-distribution tokens; you might see soft mis-sampling on rare entity names.
[01:38] Dr. Priya Rao: That's similar to what we observed — a low but worrying increase in hallucinations for certain safety-critical prompts after GPTQ-INT8. How does AWQ compare?

[01:50] Liam Chen: AWQ (sometimes annotated A-W-Q) uses per-channel scaling and a slightly different quant schedule. In our microbenchmarks AWQ had about 0.8-1.5% lower token-level perplexity regression compared to GPTQ-INT8, but it's highly sensitive to the calibration set.
[02:20] Sofia Kim: Are those numbers stable across sequence lengths? Our prefixes are often 512-1k tokens for long context chains.

[02:30] Liam Chen: Sequence length matters. AWQ's advantages shrink at very long sequences because quantization error in the KV cache can accumulate. That leads to the KV cache section: with quantized KV cache you get memory and perf wins, but there can be drift in soft-attention scores over long prefixes.
[02:55] Ethan Miles: By drift you mean attention distribution shifts and that causes different next-token probabilities? That's our main worry for downstream safety checks.

[03:05] Liam Chen: Exactly. On some tests the top-3 token set changes occasionally. For many consumer apps that's fine, for safety-critical flows it's not. We usually recommend keeping KV cache in higher precision (FP16) if you need determinism across long contexts.
[03:30] Dr. Priya Rao: Would that negate the memory savings? We need to quantify tradeoffs — maybe quantize weights but keep KV cache FP16?

[03:46] Liam Chen: That's a common hybrid approach: quantize weights (INT8/GPTQ) and keep activations or KV cache in FP16. It gives large weight memory reduction and most of the speedups, while preserving attention stability.

[04:10] Ava Martinez: On Redwood Dedicated you can configure node types; for a hybrid route we can set caching nodes with FP16 memory and quantized weight nodes for compute. That model routing is supported in our runtime.
[04:30] Dr. Priya Rao: Can you walk through an example where GPTQ fails but AWQ retains quality? We have a few safety test prompts we can share.

[04:40] Liam Chen: Sure. In one example GPTQ shifted a low-probability token to a semantically different token due to weight clipping in layer 20. AWQ's per-channel blocks preserved the distribution better. We can reproduce this with your safety prompts.
[05:08] Ethan Miles: Are there quantization knobs we can tune customer-side? E.g., per-layer exceptions, switching a few layers to FP32?
[05:17] Liam Chen: Yes; you can mark sensitive layers to remain in FP16 or FP32. We also expose a calibration set parameter. However, it's iterative; you need to test with representative prompts.
[05:35] Sofia Kim: About latency: what does INT8/GPTQ do to p50/p95 for short completions (<=64 tokens)?

[05:42] Liam Chen: For short seqs with batching off, INT8 tends to reduce p50 by 20-35% and p95 by ~15-25% on same-hardware compared to FP16. For very latency-sensitive flows we recommend optimized kernels (we use fused attention kernels) plus smaller batch sizes.
[06:05] Ava Martinez: Note: those numbers vary by model family and hardware. On V100-ish hardware FP8 sometimes performs worse due to kernel support differences.
[06:20] Dr. Priya Rao: You mentioned FP8. Is FP8 better than INT8 for quality/latency?

[06:28] Liam Chen: FP8 (e.g., E4M3/E5M2 formats) can preserve dynamic range better and often yields lower accuracy regressions vs INT8, especially for a few model families. But FP8 support is hardware and kernel dependent; on some infra it's not available or falls back to slower emulation.
[06:50] Ethan Miles: For our on-prem nodes we have Ampere GPUs and some Hopper; we need to know which path gives best perf on both.
[06:58] Liam Chen: On Hopper (H100) FP8 kernels are mature and you'll see good latency and throughput. On older Ampere hardware INT8 with optimized kernels is usually better.
[07:15] Sofia Kim: You earlier said quantized KV cache accrues error. Can we do periodic re-rolls to re-sync the cache?
[07:22] Liam Chen: Yes, options: (1) keep a high-precision checkpoint every N tokens, (2) re-encode prefixes occasionally, (3) hybrid cache as mentioned. Each has cost implications.
[07:42] Dr. Priya Rao: For safety-critical customers we might accept additional CPU work to re-encode if it reduces drift.

[07:50] Liam Chen: Also note that continuous batching interacts: longer batch windows hurt latency but improve throughput; quantization can change the optimal batching window because per-token op cost changes.
[08:10] Ava Martinez: We can run workload-aware batching simulations with your traffic profile to find the sweet spot between p95 latency and cost.
[08:20] Ethan Miles: We'll share our traffic histograms and a sample of long conversations. Expecting Bursts of ~200 rps for short windows.
[08:30] Liam Chen: Perfect. For POC we'll replicate that load shape.
[08:36] (short crosstalk, inaudible)

[09:00] Liam Chen: Thought on accuracy regressions: often it's calibration set mismatch. If the calibration set doesn't include your safety tokens (rare names, acronyms), GPTQ may quantize away small-but-important weight nuances.
[09:20] Dr. Priya Rao: We'll provide a calibration set that includes our safety/policy phrases. How big does it need to be?
[09:28] Liam Chen: 1-5k representative tokens or utterances is a good start; for best results include the rare entities and long-context examples.
[09:40] Sofia Kim: Regarding VPC/on-prem: what does Redwood require for Private deployment and KMS integration?

[09:48] Ava Martinez: For Private we can provide a control plane in your VPC or a fully on-prem package. We integrate with KMS/HSM via standard APIs; we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault. For HSM we can discuss certs and network egress rules.
[10:10] Ethan Miles: Do you need outbound connectivity for licensing/telemetry? We run air-gapped networks for some environments.

[10:18] Ava Martinez: We have an air-gapped deployment option where the control plane is customer-hosted and we ship binaries. Telemetry can be disabled; audit logs can be local only. We'll share the checklist.
[10:34] Dr. Priya Rao: Any impact of quantization on attestation or reproducibility for audits?

[10:42] Liam Chen: Quantized models can make exact bit-level reproducibility harder if kernels differ across machines. For audits we recommend versioned artifacts: store the quantized weights, calibration seeds, and runtime kernel versions. Redwood logs kernel and runtime versions in the console tracing.
[11:06] Ethan Miles: Good, we need that for compliance. Will you surface kernel ids in logs?
[11:12] Ava Martinez: Yes, per-inference trace includes runtime build id, kernel id, and quant profile id in the trace metadata.
[11:25] Sofia Kim: On the operational side, what about OOM behavior when using INT8? More memory but some ops may allocate differently.

[11:34] Liam Chen: INT8 reduces weight memory but some intermediate buffers may be larger depending on kernel decisions. We have automated placement logic to pin large activations to NVMe fallback if needed. We'll share recommended instance types.
[11:52] Dr. Priya Rao: Can Redwood do per-tenant quant profiles? We want to test different quant settings per customer in early rollout.

[11:59] Ava Martinez: Yes, you can pin model variants per-tenant. We support rollout rules for percentage-based canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback to FP16 if certain quality regressions are detected.
[12:18] Ethan Miles: That fallback sounds valuable. How do you detect quality regressions automatically?

[12:24] Liam Chen: We support automated eval hooks: you provide a test set, we run online evals on a sample of traffic. If token-level divergence or BLEU/perplexity crosses thresholds, we can automatically roll back.
[12:40] Dr. Priya Rao: Is there monitoring for hallucination patterns specifically?
[12:46] Liam Chen: We can instrument custom detectors; Redwood Optimize has a quality monitoring feature that compares flagged prompts and can trigger alerts on semantic drift.
[12:58] Ava Martinez: We should set up a small eval suite with your safety prompts for the POC.
[13:06] Dr. Priya Rao: We'll attach that to the ticket.

[13:12] Liam Chen: Quick detour to tooling: our runtime offers GPTQ and AWQ flows. GPTQ pipeline is faster to produce but sometimes higher regression; AWQ is slower but retains more fidelity on certain models. There's also per-channel quantization and calibration control exposed.
[13:34] Ethan Miles: How long does a quant job run for a 13B model?
[13:39] Liam Chen: On a 4xA100 node it can be 30-90 minutes depending on calibration dataset size and whether you're doing per-channel or layerwise tuning.
[13:50] Sofia Kim: For our timelines, we want to run a few variants in parallel.
[13:56] Liam Chen: We can spin parallel jobs on the Dedicated cluster. For POC we'll recommend GPTQ-INT8, AWQ-INT8, and an FP8 baseline.
[14:08] Dr. Priya Rao: About FP8 baseline — we've seen some models actually improve on FP8 for certain token distributions. Is that common?
[14:18] Liam Chen: It happens if the model benefits from extended dynamic range for rare-value weights. But it's model dependent.
[14:28] Ava Martinez: I'll attach prior benchmark PDFs and the shared benchmark sheet after the call. The sheet will include kernel ids and perf traces.
[14:39] Ethan Miles: One more infra question: can Redwood Dedicated run inside our VPC with private subnets and no internet egress?
[14:48] Ava Martinez: Yes, we offer a private deployment option where the control plane is in your VPC. We can also provide an offline license; telemetry is optional.
[15:00] Liam Chen: For the POC we'll recommend a small dedicated pool with mixed instance types so we can mirror your heterogeneous fleet.
[15:12] Dr. Priya Rao: On metrics, we care about p50, p95, cold-start latency (first token), and quality regressions measured on safety set.
[15:22] Liam Chen: We'll capture those. We'll also provide token-level divergence logs for top-k differences.
[15:30] Sofia Kim: Regarding KMS: we use AWS KMS but with custom HSMs. Any special work?
[15:36] Ava Martinez: We can integrate with external HSMs via PKCS#11 or vendor APIs; engineering will vet the network and certificate setup during onboarding.
[15:48] Ethan Miles: For the POC, we'd like to keep kv-cache unquantized to avoid drift; quantize weights only. Can you support that config?
[15:57] Liam Chen: Absolutely, weights quantized, KV in FP16 is a supported config.
[16:06] Dr. Priya Rao: Can we run a quick demo of token-level divergence now using your internal example?

[16:12] Liam Chen: Sure, pulling up the benchmark. (pause) Okay, showing a 1k-prefix test where GPTQ-INT8's top-1 diverged on 2.1% of tokens versus FP16 baseline; AWQ was 0.9% in same run. Note these are sensitive to the calibration set.
[16:42] Sofia Kim: Those numbers align with our observed 1.8-2.5% drift.
[16:50] Liam Chen: We also looked at generation quality: BLEU-like metric and custom safety flag count. GPTQ increased safety flags by about 1.3x on a small safety suite; AWQ was closer to baseline.
[17:06] Dr. Priya Rao: For rollout, we'd prefer AWQ if latency cost is acceptable. Is AWQ more expensive to run?

[17:14] Liam Chen: AWQ's runtime cost is similar to GPTQ in many cases, sometimes a small perf hit due to per-channel operations. For short sequences the difference is negligible, for extremely high throughput flows you might see a 5-10% throughput delta.
[17:30] Ethan Miles: What's the recommended canary strategy?

[17:34] Ava Martinez: Start with 1-5% traffic on the quantized variant, monitor metrics (p95, token divergence, safety flags), then ramp to 25/50% if stable, with auto-rollback thresholds. We'll help configure the eval hooks.
[17:52] Sofia Kim: Is there support for per-route model selection so we can route safety-critical routes to FP16 and others to quantized?
[17:59] Liam Chen: Yes, route-based pinned models are supported; you can set route policies in the Console.
[18:12] Dr. Priya Rao: About calibration sets, we will send a few hundred to a few thousand representative utterances. Any redwood format requirements?
[18:20] Liam Chen: A newline-delimited JSONL with one utterance per line is easiest; include metadata tags for safety-critical.
[18:30] Ethan Miles: We'll attach that to the ticket and the CRM.
[18:36] Ava Martinez: Great. Quick question for engineering: are there any kernel versions that are unsupported?
[18:43] Liam Chen: Some older driver + CUDA combos will force FP8 emulation and degrade perf; we list supported kernel/driver combos in the deployment checklist.
[18:55] Dr. Priya Rao: For our timeline, we'd like a POC in the next two weeks. Is that feasible?
[19:02] Ava Martinez: Yes, if you give the calibration set and traffic profile this week we can stand up the POC next week.
[19:12] Ethan Miles: We'll aim to provide those by Friday.

[19:18] Liam Chen: Operational notes: batching changes behavior with quantization. For example, if you increase batching window to 25ms you might gain 1.8x throughput but p95 could jump for short requests. We'll simulate your burst profile.
[19:36] Sofia Kim: For our latency SLOs we cannot accept p95 > 120ms. We'll mark that in the POC acceptance criteria.
[19:44] Ava Martinez: Noted. Also we'll include traffic shaping to mimic spikes.
[19:50] (phone echo, minor dropouts)
[20:10] Liam Chen: One more gotcha: some tokenization edge cases can amplify quant errors. If you have domain-specific tokenization, include examples.
[20:22] Dr. Priya Rao: We do have proprietary tokens for product names; we'll include.
[20:28] Liam Chen: Good. We'll also produce per-layer sensitivity maps so you can pick layers to leave in FP32.
[20:40] Ethan Miles: That will help. On pricing, does quantization change unit cost?

[20:46] Ava Martinez: Quantized variants reduce GPU hours and can lower cost per token. We'll send a cost model comparing FP16 baseline to GPTQ-INT8 and AWQ-INT8 variants based on your traffic profile.
[21:00] Sofia Kim: For auditing we need to ensure model artifacts (quant profiles) are signed.
[21:06] Liam Chen: We support signing quant artifacts and exposing signatures in the model registry.
[21:16] Dr. Priya Rao: Anything else on the runtime side?

[21:20] Liam Chen: We'll capture runtime traces including KV behavior; if drift appears we'll flag it. Also, for the POC we'll run long-prefix tests (1k tokens) and measure token divergence over time.
[21:36] Ava Martinez: I'll summarize and list action items now.

[21:42] Ava Martinez: Action items: Liam to provide AWQ vs GPTQ micro-benchmarks by 5/18; Ethan to share traffic profile and SLOs by 5/14; Sofia to share long-prefix tests by 5/16; Ava to send security docs and pricing by 5/13.
[22:05] Dr. Priya Rao: Thanks, appreciate it. A few clarifying q's: will the POC run in our VPC or Redwood Dedicated?
[22:14] Ava Martinez: For speed we recommend Redwood Dedicated with VPC peering for now; we can migrate to private on-prem in later phases if needed.
[22:26] Ethan Miles: Ok that's fine for POC.
[22:32] Liam Chen: We'll also include automatic rollback policies and a metrics dashboard link once the POC is live.
[22:40] Dr. Priya Rao: One more thing: could Redwood run the POC with both GPTQ and AWQ in parallel to compare?
[22:46] Liam Chen: Yes, parallel variants are straightforward; we'll pin them to different model ids and route traffic fractions.
[22:54] Ava Martinez: We'll send the pre-POC checklist and a proposed schedule after the call.
[23:02] Ethan Miles: Great. Any final questions from Redwood?
[23:06] Liam Chen: None from me, just to confirm the safety prompts and calibration set will be shared privately.
[23:12] Dr. Priya Rao: Yes, we'll upload to the secure share. Expect an encrypted bundle.
[23:20] Ava Martinez: Perfect. We'll follow up with tickets and the benchmark template.
[23:28] (brief silence)
[29:00] Liam Chen: (later in call) Quick note on monitoring: we'll provide token-level histograms, top-k divergence and safety flags per route. Those will be visible in the Console.
